newsitem.title: USA: Lockheed sets further Loral consolidation.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed sets further Loral consolidation.

text.p: Lockheed Martin Corp said Monday it was taking additional actions to enhance competitiveness against the background of significantly reduced defense spending.
The company said the actions will complete its consolidation with the defense electronics and systems integration businesses of Loral Corp.
This is expected to be completed in 1998, with savings building up to $300 million annually by 1999, Lockheed said.
There will be no material charge to 1996 earnings as a result of this plan, it said.
"Cumulatively, this consolidation, added to previous actions taken by Lockheed Martin, will drive continuing annual savings to $2.6 billion by 1999.
"Costs of implementing previous actions are proving somewhat lower than expected, and savings are likely to exceed original tartets," Lockheed Chief Executive Norman Augustine said.
Lockheed said it will close eight facilities, eliminating 2.5 million square feet of excess capacity, with a net reduction of 1,600 jobs.
This reduction will be offset by unrelated employment growth at other locations in excess of the positions eliminated, it said.
No further site closures associated with the Loral or earlier combinations are contemplated at this time, although actions could be taken to reflect future changes in the marketplace, Lockheed said.
It said the following initiatives complete this phase of consolidation:

-- Effective January 1, the C3I & Systems Integration Sector headquarters will be relocated from New York and employees transferred to Lockheed Martin's Bethesda, Md., headquarters; the New York headquarters will be closed;

-- The previously autonomous internal information systems operations in the heritage Loral businesses will be integrated into Lockheed Martin Enterprise Information Systems, providing significant economies of scale;

-- Radar, surface ship and submarine work currently performed at Great Neck, N.Y., and Bloomfield, Conn., will be redistributed to Lockheed Martin facilities in Syracuse, N.Y.; Moorestown, N.J.; and a new Long Island facility. The Tactical Defense Systems facilities in Great Neck and Bloomfield will be closed.

-- Federal Systems in Manassas is designated the Electronics Sector's lead company for combat and navigation systems for submarines and will be responsible for coordinating all new business activity in this area;

-- Weapon and combat control systems and detection systems work at Librascope, a unit of Lockheed Martin Federal Systems, will be moved to Federal Systems's Manassas, Va., site. Librascope's facilities in Glendale, Calif., will close;
-- Tactical Defense Systems operations in Manassas, Va., which perform work on mine-hunting subsystems, will report to Lockheed Martin Ocean, Radar & Sensor Systems in Syracuse;

-- Lockheed Martin Aeronutronic in Rancho Santa Margarita, Calif., will be closed and its tactical missile and electro-optical fire-control programs moved to Lockheed Martin Electronics & Missiles facilities in Orlando and Ocala, Fla., and Troy, Ala. Aeronutronic's Trident valve operation will remain in Irvine, Calif., but report to Lockheed Martin Federal Systems in Manassas, Va.;

-- Lockheed Martin Vought Systems in Grand Prairie, Texas, is designated as the Electronics Sector's lead for air defense systems and will have oversight and coordination for all current programs and new pursuits in air defense systems;

-- As part of the corporate-wide initiative to centralize procurement, a former Loral procurement operation in Yonkers, N.Y., has been combined with Lockheed Martin's central procurement to further leverage commodity costs;

-- Electronic Defense Systems will close its facility in the Bronx, N.Y., and transition operations to Lockheed Martin's existing facility at Syosset, N.Y. The entity will be known as Lockheed Martin Fairchild Defense Systems;
-- Lockheed Martin Space & Range Systems in Sunnyvale, Calif., will be integrated administratively and report to the corporation's Western Development Laboratories in San Jose;

-- Air traffic control business units, Air Traffic Management and Air Traffic Management International, both located in Rockville, Md., will be combined into a single unit, and a Paoli, Pa., site will be closed;
-- The Quintron business unit will remain based in Chantilly, Va., but will be integrated into and managed by Lockheed Martin Information Systems in Orlando, Fla.;
-- The infrared imaging business unit, Santa Barbara Focal Plane, will be integrated into Lockheed Martin IR Imaging Systems in Lexington, Mass., and its Santa Barbara, Calif., facility retained;

-- Administrative support functions in a number of companies in the Information & Services Sector's Products Group will be consolidated and an electronics assembly operation in Goodyear, Ariz., will be phased out;
-- An organizational reassignment of seven technical services units into one Services Group has been completed;
-- Consolidation of operations in Canada into a single organization with facilities in Ottawa, Ontario, and Montreal, Quebec, retained and management headquartered in Montreal, and;
-- The heritage Loral's international operations have been integrated with Lockheed Martin's international organization and all its domestic and international field offices have been consolidated.

In steps unrelated to the Loral combination, Lockheed also said it would combine several operating companies in its aircraft maintenance, modification and logistics lines of business, along with its aerostructures business, into a group called Lockheed Martin Aircraft and Logistics Centers.
The group will be headquartered at Lockheed Martin's Greenville, S.C., site.

Also in South Carolina, Lockheed Martin will close an aircraft components production plant in Charleston and reassign its work to facilities in Marietta, Ga., and Baltimore, Md., which has been renamed Lockheed Martin Aerostructures. -- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610.
